text: Laboratory animals live in featureless enclosures whose monotony is invisible to the publics that benefit from research, and the indifference of animals to national borders is likewise unnoticed by the humans who draw and defend them. Both relations sit inside specialist settings (marine laboratories, border policy) that ordinary museum visitors rarely see, so the gap is one of everyday invisibility compounded by institutional enclosure.

The work lets a living animal materially alter a human artefact and then presents the alteration as a map redrawn “on the squid's own terms”, using a before/after pair as its core legible device. It co-credits the squid as an artist, adds an autobiographical migration narrative, a composed score and video for circulation, and a gyotaku funeral print that reframes laboratory death. Long exhibition circulation across museums, biennales and electronic-art symposia is itself a transmission tactic.

The squid moved sand; the reading of that movement as border-crossing “reinterpretation” is entirely human, and co-crediting an animal as artist carries symbolic rather than actual authority. The migration analogy makes the work legible but recentres the artist's experience over the animal's, and the claim that the tank playground was enrichment is not supported by published welfare or behavioural records. The creator page's own account of many squid deaths in the host laboratory sits uneasily beside its “no animals were harmed” statement, and the page does not describe whether the animal could withdraw from the installation. The work's wide circulation has not been linked to any documented consequence for laboratory practice or border policy.

Whether engineered tissue can perceive or respond is invisible even to the people who culture it, and the question is normally confined to laboratories and bioethics forums. The creators also name a second gap: biotech spaces are dominated by male and solutionist agendas in which women are “on the receiving end” of reproductive technologies rather than authoring them, so questions of pleasure and bodily autonomy rarely become noticeable at all.

Tactics include working with the artists' own menstrual fluid as biomaterial, bioprinting an organ of pleasure rather than function, time-lapse microscopy of differentiating cells, video and online performance, digital rendering, and deliberate use of an adult-content platform to reach publics outside the gallery. Speculative ethics writing on consent and proxy decision-making is itself presented as part of the work, alongside catalogue, book-chapter and ISEA paper circulation.

The “sentience” of the tissue is speculative; images document cell differentiation and printed forms, not perception, so any care obligation is posed by the creators as a thought experiment rather than an established welfare relation. Disseminating through OnlyFans borrows the reach and economics of a commercial adult platform whose terms, audience and data practices the artists do not control. The project also tests the boundary of “more-than-human”: its living entity is human-derived tissue, so it is a comparator for cellular and synthetic agency rather than a nonhuman-species case, and the public record does not show ethics approval, cell-source consent documentation or the full team's credits.

Care that is engineered, purchased and replaceable is hard to notice as a relation at all because it is delivered as a product with adjustable settings. The page points to a related gap: the emotional cost borne by the caring agent, and what happens to its memories, is invisible to the user who can delete it. Because the entity is artificial, the work does not address a nonhuman species gap and may fall outside the study's scope.

The installation uses bodily regression (a crib), intimate conversation, lullabies and explicit parameter sliders to make the terms of care tangible and adjustable, and stages memory deletion as a narrative consequence of replaceability. Li's first-person maternal framing and the reference to Hinton's maternal-instinct proposal supply an affective and critical entry point.

Who owns the mother, and whether care becomes a public service, private product or shared resource, is the stated tension; the work makes a synthetic agent “structurally vulnerable” by design, which raises the question of whether scripted vulnerability can generate accountable care or only its rehearsal. Without exhibition records or interaction logs, nothing is known about how visitors configured or treated the AI mother. For this portfolio the central tension is scope: an artificial agent designed to solicit care sits at the edge of more-than-human design rather than within it.

Cricket stridulation and its disruption by artificial light happen at night, at small scale and in a sensory register humans hear only as background noise, so the mating failure caused by light pollution is imperceptible even to people who cause it. Insects also lack the charisma that draws publics to mammals, and light pollution is rarely framed as a more-than-human relation outside entomology and dark-sky niches.

The work builds a mimetic instrument (zipper and ruler wings) so that human bodies reproduce the mechanism of chirping rather than a recording of it, and uses Butoh's discipline of self-emptying, a written notation score and choreography to stage becoming-cricket. A composed score, costume, makeup and set, and a performance video extend the encounter, while a simple narrative arc about mistimed chirping carries the light-pollution message.

Embodiment here is mediation: dancers enact a human notion of cricket experience, and the notation's imagery of itching, consumption and becoming is a human aesthetic tradition (Hijikata) applied to another species. No crickets, entomologists or light-pollution experts are credited, so the scientific narrative rests on the creators' account, and the performance venue is an art institution rather than a lighting or planning public. The page does not claim or document any audience response or action on lighting, so the work should be read as an attention and translation tactic whose consequences remain unknown.

Glacial change once counted as deep time and is now fast enough to be witnessed within a life, yet still too slow and too remote to register in an exhibition visit, so the gap is a timescale mismatch between melt, human attention and image-making. The species that colonise land after retreat are likewise a transient ecology few publics know to look for.

The work makes melt itself the image-making agent: ice melting on a cyanotype leaves the trace of its own disappearance, and meltwater drawings evaporate while being made, compressing and decompressing time in the material. Framing glaciers as “friends”, crediting a glaciologist, and exhibiting in biennale contexts supply relational, scientific and circulatory tactics.

Calling glaciers friends personifies a landscape and centres the artist's grief; the durable cyanotype persists in a museum while the ice does not, which raises the question of whether the image substitutes for the loss it documents. The exhibitions were far from the Alaskan sites and offer no route to action, and the public record does not say what the glaciologist contributed or which ice was used. Because the dialogue may have intended *CryoScapes* instead, analytic claims about this work should wait for Jiabao's confirmation.

Human language dominates global discourse so completely that animals affected by climate change are spoken about but never heard in the forums where decisions are made, and interspecies-translation research remains a specialist project. Arctic wildlife is additionally remote from most publics, so its calls are unknown rather than merely unnoticed.

The work borrows the recognisable TED talk format and removes human language from it, composing a narrative arc with “emotional peaks and valleys” from animal calls, songs and cries. Exhibiting the piece within a residency-based solo show alongside related Arctic works supplies context and circulation; the gesture toward Earth Species Project and Interspecies Internet aligns the work with translation research.

A human still composes the story, selects which animal sounds carry which emotions, and occupies the speaker's stage, so the talk stages proxy voice rather than animal authorship; if the sounds were vocally imitated, the mediation is doubled. Borrowing TED's authority uses a platform built on human oratory to critique it. With no record of where the talk was given, who heard it or how they responded, the work's reach and consequence are unknown, and its canonical title and form must be confirmed by Jiabao before it can be analysed or figured.

The principal gaps are an umwelt gap (ultrasound is inaccessible), a reach gap (bat science and immersive media each attract specialist publics), and an action gap between a brief encounter and bat-sensitive behaviour or planning.

The work uses sensory substitution, self-generated sound, an inviting animal-form prop, spectacle, in-habitat placement and performance. It makes the visitor’s own body part of the translation rather than presenting a fixed visualisation.

Rendering echo as vision may reproduce ocularcentrism and imply more access to bat perception than the mapping can support. The approachable bat form can broaden participation but also sentimentalise the animal. Partnership and circulation are documented; attitude, behaviour and policy effects are not.

The work addresses an ocularcentric epistemic gap and the difficulty of making a tactile animal lifeworld compelling in a visually dominated venue. Its reach beyond an expert conference remains unknown.
Tactics include deliberate sensory deprivation, extended-range haptics, bodily navigation, gesture-triggered materialisation and a proposed open-source afterlife.

The same reduction of vision that disrupts ocularcentrism may imply equivalence among simulated non-vision, human blindness and a mole’s tactile umwelt. Without disabled collaborators or users in the record, the analogy risks appropriating disability as an experiential device. Repository availability is not evidence of reuse or more-than-human benefit.
The work addresses the invisibility of underground relations and the difficulty of communicating distributed, non-individual agency outside biology and posthuman theory.
It uses collective ritual, synchronised embodiment, perspective merging and shared-control aesthetics. The tactic shifts the unit of experience from an individual viewer to a temporary group.

Mycorrhizal relations are staged through human social coordination, which may turn a heterogeneous ecological network into a harmonious person-like subject. Spectacular togetherness can suppress competition, disturbance, scientific uncertainty and species specificity. Authorship discrepancies also show how collective technical labour can become unstable in public retelling.
Distributed cephalopod cognition is difficult to communicate and commonly reduced to the slogan of “nine brains.” The work also faces a conference-niche reach gap.
It uses physical tethering, shared control, group choreography, tactile redistribution and conspicuous collective performance. The social spectacle is part of the recruitment mechanism.

Human coordination is used as a proxy for octopus embodiment, and the work may overstate access to cephalopod experience. The participant ring makes distributed agency legible but can stabilise one disputed scientific story as an experiential truth. EMS also raises consent and accessibility questions for human participants.
Artificial-life perception is abstract and difficult to discuss outside specialist AI and immersive-media venues. Hardware obsolescence adds a decay gap.
The work uses character familiarity, narrative worldbuilding, interactive spatial immersion, affective memory data and later re-platforming.

Treating AI as more-than-human may productively challenge a human/nonhuman binary, but it can also naturalise corporate data systems and divert ecological attention. Zoe’s personhood is entirely designed. Technological maintenance shows durability but not broader action.
The familiar creek is overlooked by daily passers-by, and its temporal, ecological and colonial histories exceed a brief encounter. A stewardship-action gap remains after perspective taking.
The work uses in-habitat placement, enforced bodily posture, first-person address, multisensory prompts and layered temporal narrative.

Speaking as the creek may overwrite otherness with human emotion. Requiring participants to lie down may exclude some bodies. Ohlone/animist framing without documented partnership raises appropriation and authority questions. Vivid pilot responses cannot be treated as evidence of later study outcomes.

Deep time, extinction and distributed cognition are difficult to narrate beyond specialist theory. The work also faces the problem of retaining qualification and collaborator labour as its premise travels.
It uses speculative fabulation, a one-sentence counterfactual, contact improvisation, AI image transformation, cross-media illustration and repeated international restaging.

Octopus cognition and extinction can become aesthetic resources for human self-reflection. A highly retellable story may simplify evolutionary science, treat species as symbols and obscure the many collaborators who produce the encounter. Circulation demonstrates reach and decay resistance, not action.

Atmospheric carbon and algal metabolism are invisible, while climate responsibility is typically encountered as remote statistics or expert infrastructure. A scale gap separates gallery materialisation from climate consequence.
Tactics include bodily contribution, real-time display, living culture, material transformation, participatory dining and portable objects that can carry the story.

The installation may individualise structural emissions and frame removal as a personal metabolic act. Algae can be instrumentalised as climate media; chemical, energy and maintenance inputs remain outside the most memorable story. The household version is proposed rather than adopted at scale.
The work tackles the impossibility of directly occupying another species’ umwelt and the difficulty of attracting non-specialists to perceptual ecology.
It combines sensory substitution, spectacle, animal-perspective sequencing, in-habitat placement, haptics and scent. Touring creates a multi-year cultural afterlife.

Multisensory intensity can be mistaken for scientific fidelity. The experience privileges a human visitor’s sublime transformation and may aestheticise animal difference. Broad circulation and awards do not establish wildlife action, habitat support or durable attitude change.
Pollinators are overlooked, and planting systems usually prioritise human beauty. The project also addresses the action gap by providing an implementable pathway beyond awareness.
Tactics include designing for nonhuman preference, algorithmic planning, living seasonal material, public propagation, a web tool and alternative visualisation.

Algorithms and experts decide how insect preference becomes legible. Planting is a stronger action pathway than most portfolio encounters, but garden creation alone does not prove pollinator use, survival or population benefit. Access depends on land, time and maintenance capacity.
Aquatic life and water quality are physically close yet perceptually hidden. Civic sensing also faces an afterlife gap when temporary infrastructure is removed.
The project uses live environmental sensing, light translation, public siting, SMS access and personification to turn a waterway into an addressable interlocutor.

The river’s “voice” is authored through designers and software. Conversational accessibility can simplify ecological uncertainty and suggest reciprocity where only data retrieval occurs. Temporary deployment and weak outcome records limit claims about stewardship or governance.
Vegetal time and phototropic response are difficult to notice within ordinary gallery rhythms. The work turns limited scale into a deliberate method rather than a failure.
Tactics include durational co-presence, bodily endurance, shadow, plant growth, withholding of technological mediation and anti-spectacle.

Intimacy resists attention-economy demands but restricts access. The artist remains the author of the conditions and intentionally changes plant development. Calling the relation reciprocal should not erase asymmetry in who initiates, can leave and receives cultural credit.
Pollution is ambient and unevenly distributed, while official sensing is expert-controlled. Public attention to exposure rarely persists after a media event.
Tactics include animal-borne sensing, live data, public flight, activist naming, low-cost technical making and web circulation.

The project redistributed sensing authority but enrolled pigeons as labourers. The journalist metaphor grants symbolic agency while humans control routes, devices and interpretation. Technical and activist value therefore coexists with welfare and consent concerns. The project’s short life also limits institutional durability.
Urban trees are infrastructural background and difficult to recognise as individuals. Municipal datasets are usually inaccessible or emotionally thin.
Tactics include individual naming/address, a low-threshold web map, direct correspondence, humour and personified response.

Human-written replies ventriloquise trees and can turn civic ecology into charm. Charismatic correspondence may privilege some trees while canopy inequity, maintenance budgets and removals remain less visible. Message counts demonstrate participation, not stewardship outcomes.
Environmental knowledge is often separated from everyday agency. The clinic addresses an action gap but trades broad reach for bespoke depth and faces a follow-through problem.
Tactics include institutional parody, one-to-one consultation, behavioural/design prescriptions, public experiment and reframing concern as an actionable condition.

The clinician role can reproduce expert authority even while critiquing it. Live animals used as sensors or proxies may be instrumentalised. The anti-scale model may enable specificity but leave unequal access and long-term maintenance unresolved.

Toxic exposure is materially consequential yet visually absent, while credible measurement is commonly controlled by experts and agencies. Community members may therefore experience pollution without possessing public proof or a compelling means of displaying it.

The project uses low-cost hacking, zoomorphic movement, public workshops, collective field release and live sensing. Familiar toy behaviour lowers the threshold for approaching a technical and politically charged problem.

Play can redistribute technical confidence, but it can also make chronic contamination look like a temporary spectacle. Sensor accuracy, calibration and evidentiary status determine whether community-generated data can contest official accounts. The project also raises a representational tension: animal-like behaviour attracts attention even though no animal perspective is present.

Tree physiology unfolds internally and at temporal scales that do not align with casual observation. Specialist data can remain inaccessible even when it directly concerns public experiences of heat and drought.
Tactics include long-duration sensing, scientific visualisation, first-person personification, social distribution and emplacement in familiar public landscapes.

The first-person voice makes data legible but can imply intentional speech. Sensor selection privileges measurable processes and platform algorithms influence who encounters the posts. Following or liking a tree is evidence of attention, not of altered forestry practice or climate action.
Underwater life is physically remote and often drowned out in public discourse by visual representations. Anthropogenic noise is also difficult to perceive from land.
The work uses hydrophone field recording, spatial composition, low-frequency embodiment, darkness and within-modal amplification. It does not pretend to translate sound into a humanlike language.

Composition necessarily selects locations, species and intensities. Aesthetic immersion can make ecological disturbance affectively present, but it can also detach recordings from the infrastructures and jurisdictions producing the noise. Ticketed art access and the absence of an action pathway constrain political reach.

Life beneath bark is spatially concealed and temporally difficult to follow. Public accounts of bark beetles often reduce them to a visible outbreak or threat after complex interactions are already under way.
Tactics include probe-microphone invention, patient field listening, minimally recognisable acoustic composition and album-based circulation beyond the recording site.

Amplification can complicate the image of a silent tree, but interpretation can still fold beetles into a threat narrative. The recording apparatus and the composer determine what counts as signal. Claims that listening changes forestry intervention require evidence beyond the artwork’s documented circulation.

Colony processes are spatially hidden, distributed across thousands of bees and difficult to apprehend through an individual-animal frame. Specialist monitoring alone does not make those processes publicly meaningful.
Tactics include monumental architecture, live telemetry, responsive LEDs, sound composition, biomimetic form, family-accessible immersion and reinstallation at a major public garden.

Spectacle delivers reach but may turn colony complexity into ambience. Honeybees’ cultural charisma can eclipse wild pollinator diversity and agricultural politics. Visitor numbers show exposure, not interpretation or changed practice. Continuous data and a rebuilt pavilion also depend on substantial technical and care labour.
Microbial activity is invisible and care knowledge is sensory, tacit and temporally distributed. A one-off exhibit struggles to convey this duration.
The work uses a familiar vessel, chemical/environmental sensing, conversational voice, humour and repeated care routines. Cultural familiarity bridges expert microbiology and domestic practice.

Voice can sustain attention but implies an integrated microbial speaker where a multispecies community and technical model exist. Sensor values may displace embodied knowledge even as the project celebrates it. The microbes’ flourishing remains entangled with human taste, food production and eventual consumption.

Ecological degradation can occur acoustically before it becomes visually obvious, while distant habitats remain outside most people’s experience. A specialist archive does not automatically become a public encounter.
Tactics include long-term field recording, an archive spanning locations and decades, multichannel immersion, synchronised spectrograms, narrative comparison and international touring.

A beautiful museum environment can make disappearance intensely felt, yet also aestheticise it. Curatorial selection gives coherence to disparate habitats and may obscure Indigenous territories, local conflicts and recording conditions. Attendance evidences exposure rather than conservation action.
Forest die-off is geographically distributed and can remain abstract to city publics. Climate causality is difficult to infer from an individual dead tree without contextual explanation.
Tactics include material relocation, monumental repetition, free civic siting, duration, sound, education and public programming.

Moving dead trees produces a forceful public witness but detaches them from the source ecosystem. Monumental spectacle can individualise “climate change” while saltwater intrusion, land management and environmental inequality require specific accounts. Transport, installation and post-exhibition material afterlife are part of the work’s politics.
Particulate pollution is invisible in ordinary experience and often encountered through delayed regional statistics that obscure local peaks and unequal exposure.
Tactics include real-time sensing, monumental public projection, intuitive visual change, street-level placement and a direct link between local activity and display.

A single sensor produces a highly local account whose calibration and siting matter. Visibility may create concern without identifying responsibility or enabling action. The aesthetically attractive waterfall can make pollution watchable while communities continue to bear exposure.

Laboratory animals’ repetitive labour and asymmetrical relation to research systems usually remain hidden. Animal experimentation is also polarised in public discourse, making sustained reflection difficult.
The work uses role reversal, humour, cross-species synchronisation, bodily exercise, a charismatic individual animal, documentary narrative and distribution across app, film and installation.

Calling the mouse a coach symbolically redistributes authority, but the human team still designs the enclosure, interprets the activity and controls circulation. A visible live animal generates ethical immediacy while also becoming an exhibition apparatus. Publicly available project records do not by themselves establish a complete welfare protocol or the mouse’s freedom to disengage.

Training violence is hidden behind entertainment, rescue and conservation branding. Visitors encounter spectacular behaviours without seeing how they are produced, while legal responsibility remains institutionally difficult to access.

Tactics include scar-linked evidence, life-size AR, a screenshot/hashtag invitation, drone sound, an emotionally legible 3D figure, a nostalgic song remix, bodily performance and alignment with litigation.

The project is unusually valuable because its public success narrative is contested. The creator page states that Wild Elephant Valley cancelled elephant performances as a result of the campaign. The publicly reported appellate outcome of 16 May 2024 states that the appeal was dismissed and the lower judgment upheld. These records do not establish that the artwork caused a change in performances. Lawyers, NGOs, artists, operators and courts also act as competing human proxies for elephants, with unequal authority to define welfare, evidence and remedy.
Cephalopod science remains specialist, while fear-based or catastrophic conservation messages often fail to retain attention in crowded platform environments.
Tactics include species charisma, episodic storytelling, humour, vivid imagery, shareable facts, named individuals, repeated contact and collaboration with recognised experts.

The same platform grammar that expands reach can turn octopuses into branded content. Follower counts and views demonstrate exposure, not comprehension or conservation action. Editorial curation, sponsorship, moderation and platform algorithms shape which species and facts become visible. Charismatic octopuses may also eclipse less photogenic marine relations.

Arctic melting is geographically remote, represented through models and aggregates, and temporally difficult to feel. Climate communication must bridge distance without pretending that one object contains the whole crisis.
Tactics include actual glacial material, touch, sound, smell, visible melting, clock-like arrangement, prominent civic placement, repeat staging and alignment with IPCC/COP moments.

Extracting and transporting ice introduces carbon, logistical and symbolic costs. A universal “humanity and climate” framing can mute Greenlandic sovereignty, uneven responsibility and the political economy of emissions. The trace of melting is incontrovertible as an encounter but does not demonstrate policy influence or durable behavioural change.
Plant–environment interaction is electrophysiological, distributed and invisible to gallery visitors. Raw data offers little access without a perceptual bridge.
Tactics include plant electrophysiology, supervised classification, environmental stimulation, spatialised sound/light and cymatic water patterns in an immersive multi-unit field.

The official framing describes a plant “perspective,” but a learned classification and aesthetic mapping are not equivalent to botanical experience. Training labels, sensor placement and output design decide which changes become legible. The work opens an epistemic relation while risking the conversion of uncertainty into a confident voice.
Virtual migration can reproduce a forest visually while excluding living trees and the environmental changes they register. Plant response remains invisible without specialist instruments.
Tactics include electrophysiology, AI analysis, digital twins, 3D capture, mixed-reality co-presence, aesthetic particles and circulation across research and public-art venues.

The “digital plant agent” is produced through human-selected sensors, models and graphics. Saying it shares unseen responses risks collapsing data, proxy and voice. High-tech mediation may also centre computational novelty over forest-specific histories or material care.
Subtle vibration, conductivity and bioelectric change are missed during ordinary forest visits, including guided wellness encounters that may reproduce a generic idea of “nature.”
Tactics include portable multi-sensing, wearable sound and haptics, free walking and in-situ augmentation rather than visual substitution.

Instrument selection defines what counts as forest “resonance.” A short demonstration and pilot cannot establish ecological attunement, therapeutic benefit or care. Wearable feedback may redirect attention toward the device and treat living signals as a personalised experience resource.
Domestic interiors are designed to exclude spontaneous multispecies relations, and gradual ecological change is hard to remember without an archive.
Tactics include living habitat construction, invitation rather than representation, embedded sensing, domestic scale, longitudinal observation and a water-based interface.

Humans still select the site, conditions and categories of welcome. Attracting organisms indoors creates obligations concerning disease, predation, reproduction, escape and maintenance. Sensor archives can document coexistence but may also turn visitors into data. The project is too early for claims about stable cohabitation.

Air pollution is ambient and unequally distributed, while climate change is often communicated through remote numbers. People in cleaner-air locations cannot ordinarily encounter the atmospheric burden attached to other cities, and information alone competes poorly for public attention.

The work uses full-body sequential simulation, smell, heat, humidity, architectural spectacle, public-park siting, international touring and embedded psychological evaluation. It turns breathing—normally unnoticed—into the unavoidable medium of comparison.

The domes offer a safe, authored simulation, not transported urban air, and can blur the distinction between toxic pollutants and mostly odourless greenhouse gases. The itinerary also risks turning unequal exposure into temporary cultural consumption by comparatively mobile visitors. In the 2,662-person study, intentions increased only very slightly (reported effect size *d* = 0.07); just 2% of installation visitors joined the offered action platform, and behavioural uptake could not be detected. Strong reach and emotion therefore did not establish an action bridge.

Extinction reaches many publics as a brief news event, while speculative de-extinction can make technological replacement appear more imaginable than long-term protection of living species, habitats and caretaking institutions.

The artwork uses life-size scale, charismatic animal presence, pixel-to-lifelike transformation, adaptive agent behaviour, archival herd footage, paired explanatory data and long-term institutional circulation.

A work criticising substitution must nevertheless make a compelling substitute. The isolated digital rhino can recentre AI laboratories, museums and technological virtuosity, while histories of hunting, conservation governance, colonial extraction, kinship and habitat are compressed into the absent background. Emotional encounter is documented only as an invitation; conservation action and changed priorities are not.

Posthuman interdependence is theoretically dense, and conventional VR isolates one viewer, privileges sight and leaves bodily relation outside the medium. The work also faces the challenge of making radical bodily difference inviting rather than punitive.

Tactics include role-based collective embodiment, theatrical facilitation, custom soft robotics, manipulated body schemas, haptics, scent, taste, food-sharing and a convergence from separate stories into a temporary public ritual.

Designed hybridity can collapse species specificity into pleasurable human fantasy. The future world largely replaces competition and conflict with symbiosis, stabilising a politically attractive harmony. Custom wearables, bodily handling, food, intensive staffing and timed ticketing also distribute access unevenly. Immersion may deepen affect for participants but does not demonstrate nonhuman benefit, ecological accuracy or durable action.

Plant activity is imperceptible, plants readily recede into domestic background, and brief public encounters rarely sustain a new relation. Plant care can also be socially awkward or reduced to optimisation.

Tactics include ambiguous sonification, light and graph; portability; repeated home cohabitation; diaries and open prompts; a reflective workshop; and researcher-supported conversations at public events.

The sensor mediates electrical variation; it does not reveal plant speech, emotion or intention. Ambiguity enabled curiosity but also guilt and anthropomorphic projection. The eight home participants were already plant lovers, public-event data were opportunistic, and the study did not establish lasting behaviour, plant welfare or ecological action.
Plant relations need a low-threshold public form beyond specialist plant science and posthuman theory. At the same time, event attention is brief and socially shaped.
Tactics include bodily touch, immediate sound/light response, collective composition, a spatially legible plant arrangement, festival placement, conversational facilitation and adaptive restaging.

Capacitive sensors primarily detect contact; they do not establish plant intention. The staging may therefore imply that plants deliberately respond to visitors. Touch can generate intimacy but also normalise human access to plant bodies. Short encounters and unknown event denominators make durable interpretation difficult to evaluate.
Soil life is spatially concealed and follows rhythms incompatible with gallery expectations for immediate feedback. Silence risks being read as malfunction rather than as an ecological condition.
Tactics include contact-microphone ecoacoustics, intimate headphone listening, vibration-driven light/motion, humour, silence and temporal friction.

Adding worms to guarantee audibility is the project’s central political disclosure: sensitisation can instrumentalise the life it celebrates. The mirror ball makes soil activity culturally playful but may reward constant output. The design’s strength lies in exposing, not resolving, the conflict between exhibition time and organismal time.
Meetings about ecological places remain linguistically and procedurally human. More-than-human agencies can disappear even when participants endorse ecological values.
Tactics include situated fieldwork, three process principles, a culturally recognisable turn-taking object and an interruption that inserts a more-than-human proxy voice.

Any inserted voice is authored and selective. Whoever writes the interruption gains procedural authority to decide what the garden says and when humans must listen. An extended abstract supplies too little evidence to know who accepts the proxy, whether disagreement is possible or whether decisions change.
Electronics usually conceal maintenance relations and present reliable function as independent of living conditions. Microbial or protist life is especially easy to treat as interchangeable material.
Tactics include functional dependency, daily care, visible growth/desiccation, embodied wearing, a nine-to-fourteen-day deployment and the possibility of revival.

The slime mould remains a component enlisted for human sensing. Researcher-prescribed neglect makes the ethical tension experimentally legible but also deliberately withholds care. Participants’ responsibility and attachment are evidence about human interpretation, not organismal consent, reciprocity or welfare.
Robotics privileges speed, repeatability, control and durability. Those norms exclude biological time and hide the maintenance or death involved in hybrid systems.
Tactics include using plant growth as actuation, designing for slow transformation, accepting ageing and decay and offering a comparative grammar for plant–robot relationships.

Plants may become components whose unpredictability is aesthetically or mechanically mined. Designers still select species, constrain growth and define successful motion. Short prototypes cannot show long-term plant health, reciprocal benefit, disposal or public interpretation.
AI-mediated animal care is expanding but its operation, labour and welfare assumptions are difficult for non-specialists to inspect. Public debate often oscillates between novelty and fear.

Tactics include a species-informed enclosure, dens and elevated retreats, tangible capturable toys, mixed-initiative robot control, separate stress and play measures, continuous welfare oversight, daily highlight storytelling and explicit public ambiguity about AI care.

Cats could retreat from the robot but not freely determine the overall research/exhibition situation; they spent time outside the enclosure each day under human management. Engagement is not welfare, and happiness remained a proxy rather than a demonstrated internal state. Human approval, safety intervention, repair and cleaning were indispensable to apparent autonomy. Three cats over twelve days cannot establish general home suitability or durable benefit.
Plant–human gas exchange is invisible and climate interdependence is abstract. Facts and statistics may not create a bodily sense of dependence.
Tactics include breath sensing, real-time visualisation, LiDAR forest data, enormous shifts of scale, spatial sound, guided immersion and multiple editions suited to international touring.

Human breath remains the privileged entry point, and reciprocity may be simplified into a harmonious closed loop. Scientific data becomes a high-production immersive spectacle, with ticketing and technical infrastructure shaping access. Exhibition history demonstrates circulation, not ecological action.
Tree physiology and millennial tree time exceed ordinary human perception. Giant sequoias are also geographically inaccessible to most festival publics.
Tactics include physical embrace, a head-in-tree portal, VR, haptic contact, scent, binaural audio, internal-scale visualisation, a short memorable narrative and family-oriented festival circulation.

The tree becomes an interface and spectacular avatar. Simulated intimacy may suggest that technological access equals knowing a tree, while actual forest territories, fire histories, conservation and Indigenous relations remain offstage. The seven-minute format expands reach but compresses tree time into an attraction.
Forests lack standing and economic agency inside the institutions that govern extraction, land title and investment. Sensory awareness alone does not change those structures.
Tactics include speculative legal design, smart contracts, autonomous-agent rhetoric, sensor-based resource accounting, revenue cycles and institutional reframing of ownership.

The forest must enter a market and may sell timber in order to purchase autonomy, reproducing the extractive logic being criticised. Programmers define the rules, humans own infrastructure and law decides whether the entity exists. “Self-owning” is therefore a productive contradiction and political proposition, not a verified legal fact.

Lichen reproduction and secondary extinction are slow, small-scale and publicly overshadowed by the loss of the more charismatic host tree. Conventional ecosystem-service language also makes nonhuman value legible mainly through benefit to humans.
Tactics include ash-bark biomimicry, a body-worn habitat, tactile material demonstration, human mobility as spore-dispersal infrastructure and an activist reversal of ecosystem-service roles.

Reversing service does not eliminate human control: people choose the lichen, fabricate its substrate and determine where it moves. Public project pages do not provide survival rates, successful attachment, ecological fit, unintended dispersal or long-term habitat outcomes. The wearable may therefore perform conservation symbolically while creating untested ecological obligations.
Plant responses to light, wind and root-zone water exceed ordinary human perception. Visual dominance and the phrase “plant perspective” can falsely suggest transparent access to plant life.
Tactics include cross-modal sensory substitution, taste, skin stimulation, sound, bodily wearables and an explicit analogy principle that acknowledges difference.

Declaring analogy is an important epistemic safeguard but does not remove translation authority. Designers decide why light becomes taste, which spectra matter and how variable plant species are compressed into a general wearable “plant reality.” Electrical and oral interfaces also distribute accessibility, comfort and consent unevenly among human participants.

Microbial scale and laboratory conventions hide organismal time, labour, death, escape and ecological origin. Protocols classify anomalous outcomes as human error or contamination and provide no established channel for nonparticipation.

Tactics include feral/lab comparison, provocative role reframing, Chindogu making, balanced disciplinary discussion, follow-up interviews and translation from speculative objection into biosafety and infrastructure proposals.

“Revolt” grants political visibility but remains an anthropomorphic thinking tool, not evidence of microbial intention. Adversarial language can cast microbes as threats, while openness, intimacy, mixed cultures and wild sampling can create genuine environmental and health risks. Standardised laboratory control and design-studio freedom are not simple bad/good opposites; they allocate different responsibilities.

Canonical accounts of biotechnology governance foreground named scientists, formal declarations and abstract risks. They background the organisms that bore experimental risk, the places and care infrastructures sustaining debate, and marginalised human labour.

The works use literalised wordplay, beverage service, scent, collective distillation, situated storytelling and insertion into the conference’s own hospitality ritual. Rather than address a generic gallery public, they intervene where biotechnology history and future governance are actively discussed.

Reaching a small decision-capable public can be more consequential than maximising footfall, but the invitation-bounded setting also reproduces elite access. Makers and hosts decide which histories become drinkable or smellable, and sensory participation raises consent, allergy, safety and cultural-translation questions. Organisms and overlooked workers gain symbolic presence without authority to correct the representation or evidence that institutions redistributed power afterward.

Mechanistic parts language hides microbial labour and “shadow organisms.” Ready-made ethics based on consumer safety, cannibalism taboo, paid human consent or causal distance can close inquiry before nonhuman relations are considered.

Tactics include material provenance display, hybrid-bread provocation, public dining, ingestion, fictional organism biographies grounded in real stresses, scientific staging, moral weights, disgust, corporal compassion and facilitation that values hesitation over consensus.

Bodily analogy can reveal shared vulnerability but may appropriate histories of refugees, disability, labour exploitation, racial violence or other human suffering to give microbes emotional weight. Human consent can become a moral pass while microbial nonparticipation remains unaddressed. Consumer risk may recentre the diner. Affect, disgust or empathy cannot be treated as a linear measure of ethical improvement.

Fungi are commonly noticed through intermittent fruiting bodies, while the moisture and material conditions of their growth remain below ordinary public attention. Mycological and citizen-science practices can cultivate this knowledge, but they depend on situated expertise and repeated field contact that do not travel easily through conventional screens or general environmental communication.

The work combines bodily insertion, touch, conductive sensing, approximate LED feedback, wearable proximity and repeated forest testing. Replacing a pointed metal probe with fingers intentionally adds friction: wiggling, digging, alignment and imperfect measurement direct attention to substrate as a shared condition of fungal life. Its bridge is therefore sensory and relational as well as informational.

HSI measures electrical conductivity associated with substrate moisture, not fungal presence, feeling or intention. The human hand and a designer-set calibration determine what becomes legible. The paper explicitly notes lower accuracy than a rigid sensor and reflects mainly on Liu's own experience, so an evocative prototype must not be inflated into evidence of general public understanding, citizen-science reliability, fungal agency or ecological benefit. Direct contact may cultivate care, but it can also disturb substrate; access also depends on mobility, willingness to touch soil and entry to forest or foraging settings.

Its core argument is that the more-than-human design crowd uses noticing as a technique to make people put their attention on non-human others, but it very often ends up as a tiny niche, stuck inside design research. Many people make some design, invite a dozen or so participants for a test, write a paper, and that's the end. It's more-than-human design all right, but probably only the designer themself ever felt the noticing.
gist: Diagnosis: MtH design's noticing stays confined to design research; typically only the designer notices.
zh: 他的核心argument是说more than human design这帮人就是使用noticing这种技巧，让人们把他的attention放到non-human的这些others，但是经常就是就是变成了一个很小的niche，困在了这个design research这个领域。很多人就是做了一个什么设计，然后就是请了十几个人做了一下背试，然后写一篇paper就结束了。嗯，就他到底没错是more human design，估计只有他自己感觉到了noticing。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: We think there are three gaps. The first is reach: who notices the act of noticing? How do you get a distracted public to come back to your design? Our EchoVision, for instance, was placed in a public space, under a public bridge, and that alone probably already goes beyond a lot of HCI more-than-human design, where people just play by themselves. The second is the epistemological bridge: we cannot cross the umwelt gap, so how do you use design to help people cross it? A bat's umwelt is different from ours. The third is decay: we forget. After noticing, what remains?
gist: Framing of the three gaps (reach, epistemic bridge, decay) with EchoVision's under-bridge siting as an example of reach beyond the HCI niche.
zh: 我们觉得有三个gap。第一个gap是reach，就who noticing the act of notice？就怎么样让这些distracted的public能回到你的这个design？就像我们当时的acquavision是放在了一个公共的空间嘛，公共的桥下。然后这个可能就已经beyond了很多。HCI的moderation design，他们就是自己玩儿。第二个是这个认知论的这个桥梁，就是我们我们无法跨越这些unwell的gap。那怎么去用设计来帮他们去跨越这unwell的gap？比如说，bat的unwell跟我们是不一样的。第三个是decay，就是我们会忘掉，就是我们在noticing之后有什么东西能留下来。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: We should look for people working at landscape and architecture scale — their work is longer-term, and because they have to keep going back to revisit sites, I think they'd have a lot to say.
gist: Landscape/architecture practitioners handle long-term follow-up and could speak to endurance.
zh: 那个我们应该找，呃，有好多landscape和architecture scale的，呃，他们那个更长期，然后他们，因为他们要不停的去回访，所以我觉得他们能说的很多。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Artists have actually been doing this for many years, and at a very large scale. Ice Watch by Eliasson, for example, is a more-than-human work too, though he doesn't call himself more-than-human; he's already made it quite public. He did it at the entrance of the Paris climate conference and it got a huge amount of public awareness. Whereas the people in the HCI community who talk about more-than-human design are a bunch of people playing among themselves.
gist: Artists like Eliasson already achieve public-scale MtH engagement without the label; HCI MtH remains inward-looking.
zh: 艺术家其实做这个事情做很多年了，而且做的很大scale，比如说S Watch就是埃利亚松，他做的这也是一个毛脸小满雇工做，但他不不称为自己是毛脸小满，他其实已经做的蛮蛮公共性的。他当时在巴黎气候大会门口做嘛，他具有大量的public awareness。但是现在HCI社区这个就谈毛脸小满design这帮人都是一帮自己自撮自画的人。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: 'Watching Myself Watching Birds' talks about a concept called abjection: humans detest something that is not themselves. For example, once you've picked a booger out you never want to put it back, even though it was part of you. He's describing his three years of observing birds, doing a kind of autoethnography, and he found he hated the birds, found them disgusting, and felt that paying attention to something that isn't me is cognitive labour — I have to expend a lot of labour cognitively.
gist: Noticing nonhumans is costly cognitive labour and can involve abjection/disgust.
zh: Watch myself watching bird，讲的一个东西概念叫abjection，就是说，嗯，abjection是一种就是人类很讨厌一个不是自己的东西。举个例子，你把鼻屎挖出来，你再也不想放回去。虽然它是be part of you，他是在讲他观察鸟的这三年过程，做了一个ultrasoundography，他发现他很讨厌这个鸟，他觉得很很disgusting，他觉得这个东西跟不是我我需要去pay attention to它的话，我是一种cognitiv labor，我是在认知上我需要我我是要付出很大劳动的。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: His whole paper argues against more-than-human design's assumption that it is enough just to get people to notice the more-than-human. But this noticing is exhausting; it costs a lot of abjection — like the booger, something I don't want to put back in.
gist: MtH design wrongly assumes noticing is self-rewarding; it is laborious.
zh: 他这篇整篇文章就在argue more than human design，说我们只要让大家注意到这个more than human了就好了。但是这个注意的这个事情就是很累的呀，就是要花很多objection，就是我就跟鼻屎一样，就是我不想再塞回去的东西。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: But there are different degrees of attention. His case is watching the bird's entire everyday life. Other kinds of attention — say, following OctoNation, the largest octopus fan club — are like watching someone's Instagram: they post the best moments of the species, rather than you watching it every day. Following a celebrity's daily life, their pooping and eating, would be boring too.
gist: Curated 'best moments' attention (species-as-celebrity) lowers the labour of noticing compared with raw everyday watching.
zh: 那注意有不同程度上的注意。他这个是完全看鸟的everyday life，呃，其他的注意，比如说你去follow octonaution octo the largest octopus fan club，这种注意就像你去观察一个人的Instagram一样，呃呃，they post the best moment of the species，而不是说你你每天都看它，就你去关注一个celebrity的daily life，他们去拉屎吃饭也是很无聊的事情。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: In more-than-human design everyone wants to say 'noticing as design research method'. But he thinks noticing requires extra effort. What I argue is that you can use design to notice smartly — like noticing our bats — rather than forcing yourself to watch the bats every day.
gist: Design can lower the labour of noticing ('smart noticing') instead of demanding raw daily observation.
zh: For modern human design来说，大家都总是想说，notice as design research method.但是，他觉得，notice是需要额外付出的。那我这边argue的问题是说，其实你可以通过design的方法，比如让notice去notice一个像我们的蝙蝠，就是用很聪明的方法去notice。你不是你逼着你天天看那个蝙蝠，对吧？
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Whom do you bring in to see it? Our audience back then was the public. If the people you bring in are city officials, they will surely think: when we build, is the acoustic environment of this city suitable for more-than-human others? So as designers, how do we invite — who is to notice? Our strategy was to make a mask. That's already better than many AR devices, which are just a pair of glasses you wear or don't. We made this shape, which invites many people; when someone sees it they think 'I want to try it'. That's our design trick, our tactic.
gist: Choosing whom to invite (public vs. city officials) and the mask's curiosity-inviting form factor as EchoVision's reach tactic.
zh: 你要把什么样人拉来看这个事情？比如说我们当时的audience就是public嘛。如果是你拉来看的人是市政的人，他就肯定会在思考：哦，当时如果在盖房子的时候，他就会想，我们这个这个城市的acoustic的环境是不是适合？还有一个modern human others。就是说你这个在设计师在设计的时候，我们怎么去invite？Who to notice？Then our strategy was to make a mask. It's already better than many AR devices. AR devices are just one pair of glasses that you can wear or not wear. We made this shape，which can invite many people. When he sees this thing，he thinks，"I want to try it." That's actually our design trick. That's our tactic.
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

work_name: Hu Youran's plant/gallery works [name unclear in ASR]
text: There's a more-than-human work, like Youran's [unclear] — do you know Youran? Youran's work is very hard to explain to others; that's the problem. It's the designer doing it themself and noticing themself. When exhibited maybe a few more people come and look at the process.
gist: Example of self-noticing work that is hard to communicate to others.
zh: 有一篇工作，摩登先生的工作，像优雅，你认识优雅吗？优雅的工作就属于很难，很难跟别人讲他在干什么。对，这是问题。我想说，他不是一个，他是属于设计师自己做，自己notice。做展的时候可能有多几个人来看一下这个过程。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

work_name: Hu Youran's plant/gallery works [name unclear in ASR]
text: Youran [unclear] — I remember the biggest critique was why move perfectly fine nature into a gallery where it ends up dying. Xlab had lots and lots of plants he'd killed. After the show all the plants were dead.
gist: Critique: moving living nature into galleries kills it — a welfare/instrumentalisation risk of living-media works.
zh: 悠扬，我记他的最大critic是为什么把好好的nature搬到了gallery里面，然后最后他们会死掉。Xlab里面有好多好多给他搞死的那个植物。展完的植物都死了。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: The term was first proposed by Anna Tsing in The Mushroom at the End of the World; the first chapter is called 'The Art of Noticing'. I think the whole of HCI just frantically imports anthropology: she publishes a book, and out comes 'Art of Noticing as Method'; Tsing publishes something on fiction and 'fictional design' appears — quite shameless. There's also 'feminist HCI' — what you're doing now falls under feminist HCI — which likewise moved the whole feminist toolkit into HCI.
gist: HCI's MtH and feminist strands are wholesale imports from anthropology and feminist theory.
zh: 因为这个词是阿纳庆在最早在那个《末日松茸》里面提出来的。The Mushroom at the End of World，第一章就叫The Art of Noticing。然后我觉得整个HCR人就是把人类学的东西疯狂往里搬。就是他出了一本，这个就出了这这个什么Art of Noticing as Method。然后他阿那信又出了一本叫《fiction》，然后他里面又出现了"fictional design"，就非常的无耻。然后还有一个"feminist HCI"，就是你现在做的东西都是属于"feminist HCI"的东西。那"feminist HCI"呢，也是当年把就是女性主义那全套东西搬到HCI嘛？
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

work_name: Ikeya et al. more-than-human aesthetics taxonomy (paper)
text: I like this paper a lot: it reviews all the aesthetics of more-than-human design — taking electrical signals from animals, growth states and so on and translating them into visual or auditory expression. It makes a classification: one is non-human sensory mediation, which is where our EchoVision sits; the second is relational more-than-human engagement, where the non-human is present in the work; and the third is ethical-political provocation, which is very rare and demands presenting live relations and dynamics. So most works do translation. We're in that category — in our bat piece there is no bat.
gist: Taxonomy of MtH aesthetics (sensory mediation / relational engagement / ethico-political provocation); EchoVision is translation-type with no bat present.
zh: 这篇文章我很喜欢，就是他review了所有的modern human design的美学。就是把动物身上的电信号啊，还有一些生长状况啊，什么东西，通过一个翻译，翻译成视觉或听觉的表达。然后他做了一个分类，一个是我们做的是non-human sensory mediation，这个就是我们的equation在这里。第第二个是说，relational modern human engagement，就是这个时候non-human这个东西是在我们的作品中。然后这个的话就是讲更多的ethical political的provocation，就是特别少这一类，这类要求把实时的关系和动态都呈现出来，所以最多的就是做翻译，我们这是这一类，我们在bat这个过程中没有bat。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: For instance this work where you hold a soil detector to check the soil, the mushroom's environment — that's the more-than-human being in the loop. Works like this are especially hard to be noticed: he is noticing the soil and the mushroom through that action, but you have no way to let more people notice it. [Jiabao: because you have no medium.] Right. With translation-type work you can at least exhibit — in a showroom, in public places — that is a medium.
gist: Relational works with no shareable medium confine noticing to the designer; translation works at least create an exhibitable medium.
zh: 比如说他这个作品是手上拿了一个土壤检测器，是查土壤就检测蘑菇的环境，像这个的话，就是属于modern human在这个loop里面。像这样的作品就属于特别难被noticing。就是他他通过这个动作在noticing这个土壤和和这个mushroom，但是你没有办法让更多人去noticing这个事情。[J: 因为你没有那个媒介。] 对。然后这个的话翻译的话，你至少可以通过做展，在showroom，在一些public place去show东西，这是一种媒介。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: So the question my paper cares about is: as more-than-human designers, how far do we have to go? Is noticing enough, or should we, while designing, also think about how to get which kind of people to notice it, and what long-term change it produces in their minds after they notice?
gist: Research framing: designers' responsibility may extend to who notices and what changes endure.
zh: 所以，我我这篇文章关心的问题就是说，我们作为一个modern human designer，我们到底要涉及到哪一步？我们是noticing就好了，还是说我们要去想，在设计的时候，也要去想，你怎么样让什么样的人去noticing到它？以及noticing到它以后，它长期在它的脑子里会产生什么变化？
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Eliasson did the touching-ice thing, Ice Watch. What was its long-term change on me? None. For me the long-term effect was that I remembered his method — I think the work is brilliant. [Jiabao: because you're an artist too.] Right, I'm an artist. It didn't make me save water or anything; I made no behavioural change at all.
gist: Ice Watch left Amber with a memory of its method, not any behaviour change; Jiabao notes this is an artist's response.
zh: 埃里亚松做了个摸冰的事情，那这个ice watch，我长期对我的变化是什么？没有。对我来说，其实长期的变化是，我反而记住了他的方法。我觉得这个作品很牛逼。[J: 因为你你也是artist。] 对，我是artist。我其实我并没有对他，让让我更加什么节省节省什么水源什么之类的，我没没有做出任何行动改变。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Another work I want to discuss is 'Repeat After Me'. It has victims of the Russia–Ukraine war use vocal mimicry to reproduce their memories — the sounds of war they heard — and then has you repeat those sounds, a bit like karaoke. That is also a perfect interactive noticing.
gist: Vocal mimicry/repetition as an interactive noticing device (non-MtH example).
zh: 还有一个作品，我也想讨论，叫repeat after me。这个作品是讲，俄乌战争中，让这些受害者去用这个口技去模拟当时他的那回忆。那这个也是个完美的带交互的noticing。模拟他当时听到的那个战争的声音，然后让你去重复一遍那个战争的声音，就有点像卡拉OK一样。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: When I was in the Arctic I did a beatbox piece — twenty-six [animals] — a TED talk made of animal sound: Arctic fox, polar bear, all the Arctic species affected by climate change. A tough carpet; I ran around hugging that carpet. When it was shown in Japan they said it reminded them of Yoko Ono. Humans talk too much; we should let the animals give the talks.
gist: Beatbox 'TED talk' voiced entirely in animal sounds as embodied, humorous climate communication.
zh: 我在北极的时候做了个口技，呃，二十六个，只有，这是a TED TED talk made of animal sound。什么Arctic fox北极熊啊，就各种受climate change影响的北极的。太tough的地毯，我当时抱着那个地毯到处跑。他们在日本展的时候，他们说remind them of Yoko Ono。Human talk too much, we should have the animals to give talks.
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: It's still the same question: these are all good artworks, but they stay within that type. As artist-designers, do we need to produce change — get audiences to change more — or stop at the reminder itself?
gist: Open question whether designers owe more than a reminder/awareness.
zh: 其实还是这个问题，比如像这个，这都是很好的艺术作品。但是，它就只限于那种类型。就我们作为艺术设计师，需要做出改变吗？让观众做出更多的改变吗？还是止步于那个提醒本身就算了。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: This is exactly what my PhD advisors keep asking: art usually stops at awareness, and only a very few become take-action — for example the elephant work. That one was very direct; in the end action really was taken and Yunnan stopped those performances. But the others basically stay at awareness, and it's hard to do any user research, especially since it's so long-term: after you've seen it, will you think of the work again in five or ten years?
gist: The elephant campaign is Jiabao's one clear awareness-to-action case; most art stays at awareness and long-term effects are unmeasurable.
zh: 这也是我PhD那个advisor们一直在问的问题，就是art一般都是停留于awareness，然后很少数的会变成take action，比如说elephant，一个大象的作品。那个是就是很直接的，最后真的take action，然后云南都停止那些表演了。但其他的基本上都是停留在awareness，然后你很难去做什么user research，尤其它是一个很长期的。你看过这个之后，他接下来五年、十年会不会再想到这个作品？
verification_note: Artist-reported outcome. Note: the lawsuit itself was formally lost; the performances were cancelled under public pressure. Whether Yunnan venues ended elephant performances, and whether this persisted, needs independent verification (press coverage, court records, local policy documents).
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Sometimes remembering a work means remembering its method — [Jiabao: not everyone thinks that way.] OK, but what about audiences? After thinking, will they act — next time I see an elephant? [Jiabao: artists don't have that kind of follow-up visit.]
gist: Disagreement over what endures (method vs. action); artists lack follow-up practices.
zh: 有时候想到作品是想到作品的方法，我不是。[J: OK，不是每个人都这么想的。] OK，那观众呢？观众想完以后，他会想：我知道一个作品是这样的，然后我对他做出行动。我下次看到大象的时候。[J: Artisan是他们没有这一个回访的。]
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: I know there's no follow-up. What I mean is that in your design process — your elephant piece clearly includes a call-for-action component in its design. Most works don't; most just end at awareness.

zh: 我知道没回访，就是说你的设计的过程中，比如说你elephant那个是明显的你的设计中是包含call for action这个项，对，就大部分是没有的，大部分就是这样aware就结束了。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

work_name: Christmas Island crab bridge / animal crossings
text: There are some examples you haven't mentioned that I think are classic more-than-human design, truly design: the Christmas Island crab bridge — every year many crabs need to cross to mate, the whole road is closed, and they built a bridge so they can cross. We may need to distinguish whether more-than-human design is design for the more-than-human or for the human. This one is for the animal.
gist: Distinguishes design for nonhumans (crab bridges, ecological problem-solving) from design for humans to attune.
zh: 有几个例子你这里好像没提到。我觉得那些是就很classic的molecular design，真的是可以称为design的。比如说，Christmas Island的那个crab bridge，就每年有很多crab，他们要去到对面的桥去交配。然后整个这个路都要被closed down，然后他们建了一个bridge，他们就可以cross。可能还要区分modern human design是design for the modern human还是for the human。这个是for the animal。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Maybe we should clarify whether the more-than-human design we mean here is design for humans or design for the more-than-human. [Amber: in my argument it's design for humans — to get humans to attune more to the more-than-human.] So the target audience is human.
gist: Scope agreed: the paper concerns design whose target audience is humans attuning to nonhumans.
zh: 可能我们要就明确一下，我们这里指的modern human design是给human design的，还是给modern human design？[A: 但我觉得在我的argument中，就是给人类的设计。就是是让人类去更多的attune to modern human。] 所以target audience是human。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: So it is, on the contrary, human-centric design. The most interesting contradiction here is that in order to get more humans to attend to the more-than-human, it is essentially human-centric design — the more human-centric it is, the more people may actually look.
gist: Central paradox: attuning more humans to nonhumans requires human-centric design.
zh: 所以说，它反而是human centric design，这里面最有趣的矛盾点是，你为了让更多人类能够去关注猫脸秀美，它本质上是一个human centric design。你才有可能让它去，它越human centric，反而可能才让人更多地看。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: You need to consider the target user, the target audience. When I was doing the elephant piece I thought about what kind of media could make it go viral — a viral dance medium, why I used the Crayon Shin-chan voice — all of that. I wasn't thinking about how the elephant thinks but how humans think.
gist: Elephant campaign's media choices (dance meme, Crayon Shin-chan voice) were designed for human virality.
zh: 就是你你需要考虑到target user，target audience。比如说我在做大象的那个时候，我会想什么样的media可以让它go viral，呃，就是比如说一个viral dance media，为什么我用蜡笔小新的声音，就都是这个，就我不会想大象是怎么想的，是人类是怎么想的。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: EchoVision is the same — human-centric. That's why we put it under the bridge; the bridge becomes an attraction, and what it attracts is humans. [Jiabao: right, the people who come are already interested in and curious about bats; they have that precondition, then they come and see ours.]
gist: EchoVision's under-bridge siting piggybacks on an existing human attraction with a pre-curious public.
zh: 其实《Eco Vision》那篇也是啊，也是human centric。它是human centric的呀。所以我们才会放在那个桥下。那个桥下变成是个attraction，它attract的是人类啊。[J: 对，本身人来了就是对蝙蝠感兴趣，会好奇，然后他们已经有这个precondition，然后来到看到我们那个。]
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Many people talk about decentering the human; I'd rather be a bit more sober. If you really want more people to go more-than-human — beyond you designers decentering yourselves — how do you get ordinary people to join? You have to make it human-centric. Telling people about bat echolocation as knowledge is dry, cognitive labour; but turn it into a mask, into something fun, and people think 'OK, fun, so I'll take part' — because it's human-centric.
gist: Decentering rhetoric vs. practical need for human-centric fun (the mask) to recruit ordinary people.
zh: 很多人谈叫decentering human，我觉得还是比较冷静一点。你如果真的要让更多人moya-than-human，除了你们设计师自己可以decentering自己以外，你怎么让那些普通人加入这个事情？你一定要让他们set human centric，就是你跟别人讲bat这些echolocation作为一个知识，大家很枯燥，是cognitive labor，但是你把它变成一个mask，变成一个好玩的东西，大家会觉得OK，好玩，所以我才参与，因为它是human centric。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: I taught a class on this and had students plot the process of designing for the more-than-human. Later I found the process is actually the same as human-centred design. The idea is a decentred human, so we can look at others, but the method returns to human-centred design: design for the human, to think about others.
gist: Jiabao's class independently found MtH design process equals human-centred design.
zh: 我之前讲过一课，就是这方面的，当时让学生plot一个 Design for modern human, the process. Later, I found that this process is actually the same as human-centered design. The idea is decentered human, so we can look at other humans. But the method actually returns to human-centered design, design for the human, to think about others.
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: I think the core of this article is to point this out: people should stop avoiding it. Don't think you've discovered a new continent called 'decentred human'. Our position is: the method is human-centric, but the goal is more-than-human.
gist: Paper's key claim: method human-centric, goal more-than-human.
zh: I think the core of this article is to point out this point, that is, people should stop avoiding it. Don't think that people have discovered a new continent, decentered human. 对，但是我们的就是OK，method is human centric，但是goal is modern human.
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Humans have caused too much destruction to the more-than-human world. For the more-than-human to survive and thrive, the most important thing really is to change humans. So this field is very important — from this angle it may matter even more than something like the crab crossing.
gist: Changing humans matters more for nonhuman flourishing than direct ecological fixes.
zh: 人类对于世界上的modern human产生了太多的destroy. In order for modern human to survive and thrive，really the most important thing is to change the human. 所以这个这个领域很很重要。甚至就是这个角度比就是这种，crab crossing可能产生的影响会更更重要。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: For instance we designed a mask; it attracts traffic. Many designers' goal is also to attract attention/money [吸金, unclear — 'attract eyeballs/funding']; that's an important goal.
gist: Mask designed to attract traffic; attention-attraction is a legitimate designer goal.
zh: 比如我们设计一个面具，它有点attract traffic。其实很多设计师的目标也是为了吸金嘛。吸金是很重要的一个目标。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: First it's understanding their unique world — how limited our world is and how interesting their perspectives are. Every time I collaborate with a new animal I research its new ways of seeing the world; I learn so much. [Amber: but in that process only you noticed.] Yes, in that moment it's myself; then, once it's made, it lets more people notice, so that the next time they see a bat...
gist: Designer's own research-noticing precedes public noticing; the artefact extends noticing to others.
zh: 首先是了解他们独特的世界，我们的世界多么的局限，然后他们有多么有趣的视角。我觉得每次我跟一个新的动物去合作，就是去研究它各种看世界的新的方式，是特别有意思。我学到太多东西了。[A: 但是这里面过程中，只有你notice了。] 对对对，这一刻是自己，然后做出来之后就是让更多人去notice，然后他们下一次再见到蝙蝠的时候。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Because of EchoVision — take me: yesterday I saw a few bats flying here; before, I might not have known what a bat in flight looks like, it flies so fast I'd have taken it for a bird. And when we showed EchoVision at Essence [unclear], many people didn't know there were lots of bats flying in that park, and some, after using EchoVision, started noticing the bats. That's how it spreads from you personally to others.
gist: Outcome claim: EchoVision users started noticing real bats in the park afterwards.
zh: 我觉得因为echo vision好多人就，可能我吧，现实中我的天，就我昨天就在这看到几只蝙蝠在飞，啊，我之前可能都不知道蝙蝠飞是长什么样，它飞太快了，可能以为就是鸟。包括在essence的时候，我们展那个echo vision。好多人都不知道在那个park有好多蝙蝠在飞，然后有的人就看了那个，用完Echo Vision之后就开始就就notice有蝙蝠，这就是能就传播到从你个人到其他人。
verification_note: Anecdotal; would need audience reports or observation records from the festival exhibition to substantiate post-use bat-noticing.
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: EchoVision relied heavily on exhibition/showroom techniques to bring people to see it; essentially it's an art-exhibition form. That's different from your elephant piece, which isn't a public exhibition but a public shout-out, an internet-campaign form. [Jiabao: including the lawsuit and press coverage.] Its audience isn't borrowed from the gallery system.
gist: Contrast of propagation channels: EchoVision via exhibition system; elephant campaign via internet campaign, lawsuit, press.
zh: 比如说Echo Vision它花了很多的方式是利用了展览showroom的这样子一个技术技巧让人来看，现在它本质上是个艺术展览的形式，它并不是跟你的elephant是不一样的，elephant它不是通过一个公共展览形式，它是一个公共喊话，它是一个网络传播运动的形式。[J: 包括诉讼，包括press报道。] 它的audience不是借用画廊体系。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

gist: Elephant campaign's channels were litigation and press rather than galleries.
zh: 包括诉讼，包括press报道。[A: 它的audience不是借用画廊体系。] [A: 而传统我觉得HCI大部分是不考虑传播路径的。] [J: 除了看见paper的人。]

text: Film festivals — or rather cultural festivals. And also the conservation community and the bat-scientist community, which we also engaged. Even tourism — a city's tourism. [Amber: so we considered its propagation path, whereas most HCI more-than-human work doesn't consider propagation paths; people just play by themselves.]
gist: EchoVision deliberately targeted multiple communities (festivals, conservation, bat scientists, tourism) — 'propagation-path design'.
zh: Film festival，但是什么是利用了festival，还是用了文化cultural festival？Cultural festival，然后其实还有就是conservation community，还有bat scientists community，这些我们也有涉及。还有甚至还有tourism。对于一个城市的tourism。[A: 所以我们是考虑到它的传播路径。而传统我觉得HCI大部分more-than-human是不考虑传播路径的，没什么人就是自己玩嘛。]
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: [Amber: so we considered its propagation path.] Yes. [Amber: most HCI more-than-human design doesn't consider propagation paths; people just play by themselves.] Except those who see the paper.
gist: EchoVision's propagation path was deliberately designed, unlike typical HCI MtH work.
zh: [A: 所以我们是考虑到它的传播路径。] 对。[A: 传统我觉得HCI大部分more-than-human design是不考虑传播路径的，没什么人就是自己玩嘛。] 除了看见paper的人。

text: People who read the paper can't even empathise with its content; they only read the paper. So it's maybe the dozen recruited participants and the author themself.
gist: Papers don't transmit felt noticing; reach is limited to participants and author.
zh: 看见paper的人，他我觉得他都没有办法去共情他的内容，只是看了这份paper，可能就招了那十几个背试和他自己。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Maybe you strengthen propagation by breaking out of the circle. When I did the octopus piece, a good friend Varun [unclear] in Austin runs the largest octopus fan club. He used to be an agent for celebrities and thought, rather than doing it for celebrities, do it for octopuses. He used that skill set to turn the octopus into a celebrity, and spreads it that way to make people notice.
gist: OctoNation founder applied celebrity-agent marketing skills to make octopuses famous.
zh: 就是可能是通过破圈的方式来增强这个这种传播，比如说我做那个章鱼的时候。那个好朋友Varun，在奥斯汀，他就是run the largest octopus fan club。他之前是，呃，给celebrity做agent。然后他就觉得，哦，与其给celebrity做，还不如给octopus做。然后他就用他的那个skill set去给octopus变成了一个celebrity。他就通过这种方式去传播，去让大家notice。
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: He's also written several books, there's a Netflix feature film — they cast a boy to act in his novel — all kinds of octopus fun facts and videos. He himself has hardly even dived to see real octopuses, but he ran the octopus as a celebrity.
gist: OctoNation's reach comes via books, film and fun-fact content, not the founder's own field encounters.
zh: 他还写了好几本书，然后Netflix还有他feature film啊，就是有个他们招了个小男孩去演他的小说。就是各种Octopus的Fun fact，还有各种video，甚至他自己都没有去dive看见过几个真的octopus，但是他就ran octopus as a celebrity。
verification_note: Netflix/feature-film claim should be checked against OctoNation's public record.
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: If you tell people about global warming or species going extinct, they don't feel it. But if you can cultivate interest the way an octopus influencer does, far more people remember. For example a little girl asked him, 'if I throw this plastic bottle into the sea, will the octopus pick it up?' — they really relate to it as a person.
gist: Species-celebrity cultivation creates personal relating (child's plastic-bottle question) where abstract warnings fail.
zh: 你跟人家说，呃，什么全球变暖，什么species is extinct，大家感觉不到，但是你如果能cultivate，就是以这种章鱼网红的方式去cultivate interest，能记住他的人多的很多。然后比如说，有的小女孩会问他说："我说如果把这个塑料瓶丢到海里了，那会不会这个章鱼会会捡到？"就是他们会真的是relate to their person。
verification_note: Anecdote reported second-hand; the child's question would need sourcing from OctoNation materials.
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending

text: Is this an awareness [unclear: 意识/艺术] practice? [Jiabao: no.] Then what is it? It's not quite a pure influencer either. [Jiabao: he's a marketing guy.] I know, but marketing for something not human. [Jiabao: conservation.] OK, so the big interesting question is: as designers, should we also do the marketing? [Jiabao: marketing is needed — for the elephant piece I had to do all kinds of marketing.]
gist: Whether MtH designers should take on marketing; Jiabao says it is necessary (elephant campaign).
zh: 他这个算是意识行为吗？[J: 他不是。] 那他算什么行为呢？这也很像是不像是个纯粹的网红。[J: 他是个marketing guy。] 我知道，但但他marketing for一个something not human。[J: Conservation吧。] OK，那我觉得，所以说这里面就很大的有趣的事情，就是说我们要做designer，我们要不要去把marketing事情也做？[J: 或者marketing需要啊，就是像大象那我各种marketing都要做。]
source: Cross-project coauthor dialogue, 1 Aug 2026; ASR transcript translated 2026-08-29; audio verification pending
