text: Hospitality has politics. The humans still decide who is welcome: mosquito larvae, a predator that eats the visitors, a plant that outcompetes the rest, and the page's "multi-species cohabitation" is a curated guest list whether or not it says so. Attracting organisms indoors creates obligations, disease, escape, reproduction, death, that a household carries with no welfare officer, no ethics board and no protocol, which is the flip side of leaving the gallery: the welfare risk moves somewhere nobody is looking. Cunha and Mancini's point about the day after applies with force here; an enrichment that ends abruptly is a harm, and a pond in a rented flat has an ending date the residents may not control. The sensors turn visitors into data for research and exhibition, so the pond is also a laboratory, and the organisms are participants who did not enrol. I side with Youyang against the gallery critics on the direction of travel, but I would want the care plan, the unwanted-arrival rule and the closure plan written down before I called this a model. text: Pollution Pods crosses the two bridges most MtH-HCI work never reaches — a public park in Trondheim, Somerset House, later WHO and UN rooms — and then documents its own failure at the third. Sommer and colleagues questionnaired 2,662 visitors: intentions rose from 2.62 to 2.69 on the scale, d = 0.07. The behaviour measure was worse. In Trondheim every visitor got a login code for the Ducky carbon-tracking platform; 24 people, two per cent, ever logged in, so no behaviour could be analysed and London dropped the measure. That is the awareness–action gap stated as a number, and I respect that they printed it. The other gap is the noticer. The people who breathe Delhi's or São Paulo's air are represented inside the domes but never encountered by them; the visitors are mobile Europeans with clean lungs, and the decision-capable actors who could change emissions policy met it as a lobby exhibit. Reach and epistemic bridges: crossed. Action: measured and absent. Decay: it tours, which keeps the object alive, but nothing in the study says anyone remembered it a month later.
gist: Reach and epistemic bridges crossed at scale, action bridge measured and found absent (d = 0.07, 2% platform uptake), affected publics represented but not encountered.

text: Three tactics I would borrow outright. First, the invitation outfit: five geodesic domes in a park are a visible promise before anyone knows what is inside, and the sequential route means you cannot sample one city without walking through the others. Second, embodied juxtaposition through breathing — you do what a Delhi resident does at your own scale, with safe substances, heat and humidity standing in for the toxins; it is the same mechanism as echolocating with your own voice in EchoVision, and it works because the body cannot refuse to breathe. Third, the thing MtH designers skip: they built evaluation into the commission through Climart, with baseline and exit questionnaires and a behavioural channel. Where I would have done it differently is the channel itself. Handing out a browser-only login code at the exit is a propagation-path mismatch; Sommer's own discussion says the step was too big. The call-for-action should be executed at the dome door with a research assistant, or aimed at a named noticer with leverage — an air-quality regulator — instead of a diffuse public asked to log showers.
gist: Iconic architecture as invitation outfit, breathing as embodied juxtaposition, evaluation baked into the commission; the action channel was a browser-only mismatch that should have been executed on site or aimed at a regulator.

text: This is the reach–depth double bind with the numbers attached. The spectacle recruited thousands and the immersion produced sadness, helplessness and anger, which the study links to intention change, and still the effect was d = 0.07. The honest reading is not that the work failed but that awareness was never going to be action, and I would rather the field cite this than keep implying the opposite. Two further tensions. The domes let comparatively wealthy, mobile visitors consume other people's exposure for twenty minutes and leave; the affected publics are a scenography. And the safe simulation blurs what it claims to translate — smoke, scent and heat stand in for both particulate pollution, which you can smell, and greenhouse gases, which you cannot, so the felt equivalence is a designed fiction. I disagree with nobody on the note, but I would push the conclusion: the strongest evidence in this whole portfolio is negative evidence, and that makes Pollution Pods more useful to us than any work whose creator reports impact without a denominator.
gist: The double bind quantified: spectacle recruits and moves emotion but not behaviour; mobile visitors consume represented harm; simulated air conflates smellable pollution with odourless CO2.

text: Reach is not the problem here: Cooper Hewitt commissioned it, took it into the permanent collection, and it has since sat in the Natural History Museum in London, Bern, Onassis Stegi and the Biennale of Sydney. text: The tactics are charisma, scale and a punchline. text: The tension I would name first is whose intelligence is on the wall. The rhino learns like a reinforcement-learning agent because it is one; the behaviours are adapted from Policht's footage, but the mind is DeepMind's. So the work critiques technological substitution by staging a very good substitute, and the affect it produces — grief for a creature that is visibly artificial — may attach to the virtuosity of the simulation rather than to the absent animal. The note says this recentres AI labs and museums; I half agree. The paired data screen is exactly the disclosure that stops it becoming false fidelity, and I would rather have a work that shows its mapping than one that hides it. The unresolved politics are elsewhere: the hunting, the horn trade, the colonial and conservation history that produced two surviving females are compressed into a wall text, and the rhino is alone in a white room without a habitat to argue for. Charisma bias is the price of admission — nobody would commission The Substitute for a snail — and I would pay it, but I would not call the documented emotion evidence of anything beyond the gallery.
gist: A critique of substitution that works as a compelling substitute; the agent's mind is DeepMind's not the rhino's, though the data screen keeps the mapping honest; charisma buys reach at the cost of habitat politics.

text: This is the invitation outfit as a whole production: choose your creature, be dressed in a soft-robotic haptic suit by a host, smell the forest, eat a Michelin-designed snack tailored to your species. It is the bat mask multiplied by five senses, and it recruits people who would never read a posthumanist paper. The mechanism, in Polymorf's own words, is that VR blinds you and touch relocated across the body disturbs your orientation, so the brain rebuilds a body schema from what it is given — embodied juxtaposition by sensory substitution rather than by doing what the animal does. I rate the refusal of ocularcentrism highly; most VR MtH work is eyes only. The tactic I would borrow is the ending: separate inner monologues converge in a collective eating ritual, which turns a private trip into a shared event people can retell together, and the producer reports that dialogue starts at the table. What I would do differently is give that table an ask. Symbiosis stages coexistence as a feeling; nothing in the design routes the feeling to a practice, a place or a decision, and after the suit comes off the somatic ritual has no carrier.

text: The double bind is written into Polymorf's own statement, which says that translating VR into an embodied multisensory experience makes it more human-centred, more intimate, more emotional. That is exactly right, and it is the problem: the charisma that sells out Museumnacht is a harmonised Symbiocene where hybrids share resources inclusively and conflict has been edited out. Real symbiosis includes parasitism and predation; a future without them is a comforting fiction, and comfort is not defamiliarisation. The slime mould has a voice actor. So does the toad. Who speaks for the nonhuman here is a scriptwriter, and the alterity on offer is a human inner monologue wearing a species name. I also count the access cost: custom wearables, bodily handling, food, hosts and tickets mean the work is available to a few dozen people a night in cities with festivals. None of this makes it bad art; it makes it a test case for the paper's claim that human-facing means can serve more-than-human ends only if the ends are specified, and here they are not.
gist: The makers say multisensory VR makes the work more human-centred; the Symbiocene fiction edits out conflict, nonhumans are scripted voices, and the intensive format restricts access to a few dozen people a night.

text: The paper says the device offers a one-to-one representation of the responsivity physiologically present inside the plant, and four pages later admits it shows that the plant reacts, never what it reacts to, and that this gave participants a false sense of being able to communicate. Both cannot stand; the second is true and the first is the false-fidelity claim our field keeps making. The sensor mediates electrical variation through an EMG circuit and a sound designer's choices. The anthropomorphism it produced is real and interesting — Ellen felt it morbid to cut salad, Louise forced the plant to react by touching its leaves when it ignored her music and felt bad — but the authors read guilt as affectionate care, and I read it as the valuation gap turned into feeling with no practice attached — Webber's result again: perception shifts, care behaviour unmeasured. Louise's episode is also a welfare story: the design gave the plant a voice, then gave her the means to make it speak on demand, the instrumentalisation translation devices invite. The stigma finding — Allan hiding to attach electrodes to a tree — is the most political thing here and deserves its own paper.

text: Plant Sensorium reaches further than Plant Radio and translates less. The venues are good — SEEK festival on a public marina with 9,000 visitors, Maker Faire with 6,500, Processing Day — and roughly 380 people entered the frame for one to ten minutes. But the authors state plainly that the responsivity is not based on the plant's internal signals; each pot is a capacitive touch sensor with a unique sound. Nothing of the plant is sensed. The plant is a switch, and what the visitor learns is which switch makes which tone. That is why the paper concedes exhibition relations were more superficial and that the plants became a medium to talk about the design. So the umwelt gap is not narrowed here; it is decorated. The one exception is real: at SEEK the plants triggered without anyone touching them, from wind and insects, and that moment did what the rest could not, by showing a composition nobody human was making. After the festival the twelve pots go home with the researchers and the everyday invisibility of plants resumes for everyone who walked through; nothing was designed to follow them out.
gist: Good festival reach for a few minutes each, but the sensor is a touch switch that senses nothing of the plant; only the wind-and-insect triggers were genuinely more-than-human, and nothing follows visitors home.

text: As an invitation it is efficient: a walk-in wooden frame, twelve plants with green LEDs, no instructions, so the affordance is discovered by touching, and the reward is immediate sound. Responsivity produces curiosity, which the authors say outright, and the lingering ethereal sound design is what keeps people in the frame. Collective composition is the tactic I would keep — two or four strangers making a soundscape together turns a solitary demo into a small ritual, and the engraved question, if Mother Earth could sing, is the kind of humour that gets someone to step in. Restaging across three very different events with a facilitator hovering rather than presenting is good practice. What I would have done differently is make the nonhuman players the point. Wind and insects already play this instrument; I would design so that most of the time the visitor is listening to something else performing, and their own touch is the intrusion. That inverts the mechanism from human-triggered responsivity to noticing an ongoing composition, which is closer to what plants and soil actually do, and it is a cheaper honesty than pretending capacitance is plant intelligence.

text: Plant Disco is the timescale mismatch as a design object. The paper's own account: plug the contact microphone into soil and in most cases you hear almost nothing at first, because the probe disturbed the insects or the weather is wrong; the device needs to be left for days, weeks or months while the soil settles and patterns emerge. Then they took it to a design showcase where each visitor had about two minutes. The intended noticer — someone with a garden, balcony or houseplant who checks the mirror ball daily through the seasons — has not yet been reached; the evidence in the paper is the authors' own prototype testing and conversations at one exhibition. This is close to the case in which only the designer noticed, and I say that with sympathy, because soil is genuinely slow and the idea came from a botanical-garden volunteer who wanted to appreciate plants in their extended season. The labour is real too: installing it means flipping stones and staring at dirt to find a lively patch. That is Biggs's tedium, which the authors treat as productive, fairly, but it is a cost a two-minute public will not pay.
gist: Soil needs weeks to be heard and the showcase gave visitors two minutes; the intended garden user has not yet been reached, so the evidence is the designers' own listening.

text: The mirror ball is the tactic and it is a good one. text: Twenty-four worms. To make soil perform on a two-minute exhibition clock, the designers moved composted garden soil into a plastic box, added plants, leaves, sticks and two dozen earthworms, kept it wet, amplified the signal and tuned the sound profile to maximise its potential. They write that this went against their own principles, that they instrumentalised the worms and trapped soil in human time. I believe them, and this is the reach–depth double bind in its purest form: the reach event demanded the depth be faked. Two things follow. First, the confession lives in a DRS paper the showcase visitors will never read; accountability to the public was displaced into accountability to reviewers, which is the paper-driven inwardness I complain about, practised even by the reflexive. Those are the welfare and ending questions a garden deployment would force.

text: The tactic is procedural rather than sensory: a turn-taking object everyone recognises, which makes it an invitation outfit for governance, and an interruption that gives the garden a slot in the agenda. The mechanism it relies on is that meeting rules are cheap to change and hard to ignore; if the stick has the floor, the humans wait. I would borrow the move wholesale and relocate it — into a planning committee, a developer's site meeting, a university estates board — because the leverage is in who is obliged to listen, not in how well the garden is voiced. Two changes I would make. The voice should be carried by something the humans cannot have written: a soil moisture trace, a bird count, last week's frost, so that the interruption is data the meeting must interpret rather than a script the designers composed. And it needs a decision trace: minutes recording what the stick said and what happened next, which is the follow-up obligation a design-research prototype can meet cheaply and an extended abstract cannot report. The three principles — consideration, connectedness, dynamics — are fine, but principles are what the field already has too many of.

text: Whoever writes the interruption speaks for the garden, and a talking stick makes that authorship invisible by borrowing the authority of a ritual. text: This is the one work in my group with a utility function, and that is why it matters. Heart-rate sensing only works while the slime mould is alive and conductive; care is the price of a feature people already want. That answers the critique I made of the mushroom-soil probe, which asked the user to notice for the mushroom's sake with nothing in it for them. Here noticing is paid for, and it recruited a routine within days. The second tactic is embodied juxtaposition in miniature: water and oats twice a day, the same things the wearer eats — P1 checked the watch whenever she fed herself, and P5's partner, feeding her oatmeal while she was ill, called her my little slime. text: The welfare tension is built into the design: to study care the researchers prescribed neglect, and the organism dried out in under two days on five wrists so guilt could be recorded. The paper is scrupulous — dormancy, not death, resuscitation possible — but participants called it dead, and a design that treats letting-die as a phase in an interaction cycle has made harm a UX primitive. I am relaxed about Physarum's sentience; on Levin's spectrum it sits far from suffering, and the dependency here is real rather than staged. The subtler problem is that care becomes a feature, a Tamagotchi with a pulse, and the affection attaches to the device — my little friend, the little pet — rather than to slime moulds in the world, which the paper never asks about. The all-women sample, citing girlhood toys, is flagged by the authors; care work is gendered labour and a care-based interaction that recruits only women has learned something about its own politics. I would not call this a critical living-media case, as the note does. I would call it the clearest Action-side tactic in the group, with a welfare cost it names and does not resolve.
gist: Prescribed neglect makes letting-die a UX primitive; care becomes a device feature attached to the watch rather than to slime moulds anywhere; the all-women sample exposes the gendering of care labour.

text: I read the abstract and the authors' summary, not the paper, so I am annotating a design-space contribution: primitives for plant-driven actuation, proof-of-concept prototypes, measurements of the forces plants exert. That is the literal case of only the designer noticing, and I do not hold it against the work, because it is enabling research rather than an intervention and does not pretend otherwise. The gap is one of category. The timescale mismatch is also the substance: robotics wants immediacy and repeatability, plants deliver slow change and decay, and the abstract frames that as an alternative design principle rather than a problem to be engineered away. text: The tactic is to make the nonhuman the actuator. If the plant does the moving, the robot's temporality is the plant's, and slow growth, ageing and decay are built into the artefact rather than represented to a viewer; the noticing is structural, not performed. That is a decay-bridge tactic in reverse — a device designed to fall apart on a biological clock, its ending written in — and more interesting than most temporality rhetoric because it commits hardware to it. The second tactic is the design space itself. A comparative grammar of primitives with force measurements is a transmissible artefact for engineers, and engineers are the decision-capable noticers I keep naming; a plant that can push a gripper is an argument a roboticist can use, where a paper about plant-blindness is not. What I would do differently is move one prototype out of the lab and let it age in public — a robot in a foyer that visibly greens, stiffens and collapses over a semester is a story people retell, and the fact nugget, that a seedling exerts enough force to move a mechanism, seeds curiosity. As it stands the mechanism is proven and the noticing is hypothetical.
gist: Making the plant the actuator builds decay into the artefact; a primitives grammar with force data reaches roboticists, who are decision-capable; one prototype aging in public would give it a story.

text: A plant-robot hybrid is a harness by another name. The designers select the species, constrain the growth, decide which motion counts as success, and read decay as a design quality; the plant is a component whose unpredictability is mined for aesthetics and for a paper about alternatives to control, which is a control of its own. I would put that plainly rather than hide it, because the honest counterargument is also strong: robotics already instrumentalises steel and lithium, and a plant actuator at least makes the dependency on living matter visible and lets it end. What the abstract does not say, and what I would want before calling this more-than-human, is who waters the robot, what happens to the plant when the prototype has served its proof of concept, and whether decay here means the plant dies on schedule for the demonstration. Growth aestheticised is still growth extracted. The legibility question runs the other way from my usual worry: nothing here pretends to access a plant's perspective, so false fidelity is absent; the risk is that the plant is legible only as force, and force is the most anthropocentric reading of a plant there is.
gist: A hybrid that is a harness: species chosen, growth constrained, decay aestheticised; honest about dependency on living matter but silent on watering, disposal and whether the plant dies on schedule.

text: This is the welfare-protocol benchmark, and the protocol is the tactic. text: The mechanism is embodied juxtaposition done through breath. You do not watch the tree breathe; you breathe, and the system draws your exhale into the tree's flows, so your body performs the interdependence rather than being told it. The fact nuggets are strong and I have caught myself retelling them — mice can live in a sealed jar if there is a plant inside; 2,700 litres of oxygen-laced blood a day; "who is breathing who?". What I would borrow for Reality Design Lab is the breath interface itself, because breath is the one embodied act every visitor already knows how to do, so the noticing labour is near zero. text: The tension here is legibility versus alterity, and MLF chose legibility. The forest is drawn as a mirror of the human cardiovascular system — capillaries into phloem, mitochondria into mycelium — which is beautiful and makes the sequoia comprehensible, but it is a human template laid over a plant. The tree is legible because it has been made to look like us. The researcher note says reciprocity "may be simplified into a harmonious closed loop"; I would say it flatly is, and that the harmony is the price of the reach. There is also the platform question: this work lives or dies on ticketed institutions with VR infrastructure, so the public it can compose is whoever those institutions already admit. text: terra0 has no sensory bridge at all, and that is the point: nobody perceives the forest, they read a white paper. The epistemic object is an institution, property, not an organism. Its Reach is real but specific: the 58th Carnegie International, the Venice Architecture Biennale, the CCA, The Shed, plus Forbes and Süddeutsche Zeitung headlines, which means it reached lawyers, architects and crypto people, closer to decision capacity than most gallery publics. The bridge it fails is Action, ten years on. The 2016 paper's scenario, a forest selling logging licences through smart contracts until it repays its token-holders and becomes sole shareholder of itself, has never been executed; the site still lists "Autonomous Forest (2025 | tba)," and the later works are reflections on the claim rather than the claim. Decay is the odd one: the concept is retold constantly, so transmission is strong, but institutional persistence, the thing it promises, depends on a blockchain and on a court that has not yet ruled. The action available to the forest, notably, is to log itself.

text: The tactic I want from terra0 is institutionalisation as a decay mode: encode care in a contract so persistence does not depend on a designer's continuing attention. Our installations get orphaned when we stop paying for the server; a smart contract is at least an attempt at a maintenance owner that is not a person. Related, and better: Two Degrees (2021) is an artwork that burns itself when global temperature passes 2 °C, which is a responsible ending written into the artefact as a clause. The white paper's other move is genre: it is a crypto white paper, a propagation path into a non-art public that already reads that form. And it is meme-grade retellable, "a forest that owns itself by selling its own logging licences," one sentence, no experience required, exactly like Ice Watch. A tree; a corporation; a person (2022) then tests legal personhood in a US jurisdiction, which is a decision-capable noticer chosen on purpose. What I would do differently is pair the institutional bridge with a sensory one, so the forest is something a person has stood in, and state which court, which land, which contract, so the claim can be checked.

text: Lichens are the least charismatic organism in this portfolio: no face, no motion, no sound, and a secondary extinction that rides invisibly on the far more legible death of ash trees. Habitate got them into Dutch Design Week and the STARTS circuit, which is reach into a design public, and the one-sentence retell is strong — wear a tree's bark so lichens can hitch a ride. The action bridge is where I look hardest, because this is the rare MtH work that specifies the actor: the wearer disperses spores by walking. But the project page gives no evidence anyone wore it outdoors beyond the festival, no attachment or survival counts, and no ecologist's verdict on whether human-carried propagules of a chosen species help or harm; Chen's collaborator list includes lichenologists and ecologists, so the question was askable. So the invitation is crossed, the epistemic bridge is a tactile material demonstration, and the action and decay bridges are proposed rather than walked. text: The inversion of ecosystem services is the tactic, and it is a good one-sentence provocation: humans providing habitat and dispersal for a nonhuman rather than the other way round. The wearable does three jobs at once — an invitation outfit, since bark-textured clothing gets a festival visitor to stop; a literal habitat, since the material mimics ash bark's porosity, light permeability and pH; and a routing of action through the artefact, since the ask is nothing more than walking outside. That is the cheapest call-for-action in my group, and the biomimicry gives it a fact nugget people can carry: ash bark has a pH lichens need and other trees do not. Working with lichenologists is the triangulation I want. What I would have done differently is the return visit. A conservation claim needs a count — wearers, walks, thalli attached to anything — and I would have put that count on the garment. Without it the mechanism is a metaphor of care, fine for a festival and useless for a lichen. I would also have handed the garment to people who already walk in ash woodland daily — rangers, dog walkers — rather than designers.

text: The overclaim risk is in the vocabulary. Participatory conservation, ecosystem services, secondary extinction are the words of a discipline that counts survival, and the project borrows them without the counts, so a speculative garment reads as an intervention. The second tension is biosecurity, and it cuts against the work's own good intentions: humans deliberately dispersing propagules of a designer-selected species is precisely what conservation biologists worry about, and reversing the service does not reverse the control — people still choose the lichen, fabricate its substrate and decide where it travels. The wearer bears no risk; the ecology might. Third, paternalism toward the human public: the design asks strangers to become infrastructure for an organism they cannot see, which is noble, and it asks it in a festival where the commitment costs nothing, which is where noble asks go to die. I think Habitate is one of Chen's most honest works precisely because the action is specified enough to be checked, and the politics I am naming are the politics of being checkable. The intentional absence I would accept is deployment; the absence I would not is the survival number.

text: The public here is twenty-eight biologists and designers in three workshops, sixteen interviewees, and CHI. By my usual test that is a niche; by the test that matters — is the noticer decision-capable? — it is the right niche, because these are the people who hold the pipettes, write the protocols and manage the biosafety cabinets. A biologist who reconsiders what a contaminated tube means has more leverage over microbial lives than a gallery of thousands. The gaps are downstream. Nothing in the paper shows a protocol, lab rule or procurement decision that changed; the outputs are sketches on a canvas and five implications addressed to regulators who were not in the room. The twenty-four Chindōgu were not exhibited, so no public saw the squirting pipette or the biodegradable petri dish, and the interviews record how designers navigate rules, not any organism faring differently. text: Three tactics worth stealing. The feral-versus-lab journal is embodied juxtaposition done in the imagination — write your organism's habitat, death and fulfilment twice, then read the difference — and it surfaced the epistemic split the paper is really about: designers romanticise the feral, biologists defend the lab as safe. Third, and rarest, the follow-up: sixteen interviews that turn a provocation into named infrastructure — flexible sterilisation, documented traffic maps of organisms and waste, liminal rooms between studio and biolab, regulators treated as enablers. That is routing to action for a specified actor, the lab manager. What I would have done differently is materialise and exhibit the twenty-four objects, in a biosafety cabinet, at a science festival, so the tactic has a shareable medium beyond a CHI figure; and I would run the workshop on the regulators themselves, since the paper names them and never convenes them.

text: Revolt is a thinking tool, and the paper says so, but it anthropomorphises death, low growth and contamination into intention, and the biologists heard anarchist threat where designers heard unmet need. That divergence is the real finding, and it shows who speaks for E. coli: designers who mostly have not cultured it, reading refusal into events a microbiologist calls Tuesday. The romance of the feral is the paper's blind spot, exposed by its own participants — the Madagascar cockroaches released in Hyde Park as care are what happens when care is felt without ecology, and the interviewee who says people think lab rules stop at the lab door describes a biosafety risk the revolt frame encourages. I disagree with the note only in emphasis: it calls this one of the strongest complete RQ1–RQ3 cases; I call it the strongest RQ3 case because it argues with itself — lab control and studio freedom are, in the authors' words, different allocations of responsibility, not good and evil. I side with the biologists on consent: a microbe cannot revolt on your behalf, and a lens granting it a moral conscience for workshop purposes should not later be cited as evidence of one.

text: The smallest public in my group and possibly the most consequential: the delegates of a conference convened by Rice, Stanford and the Science History Institute at the Asilomar grounds in February 2025 to revisit the 1975 recombinant-DNA meeting and debate AI, pathogen research and containment. text: Three tactics, all portable. Siting: go where the decision is being made and insert the work into the institution's own hospitality ritual, so that nobody has to choose to attend — situational immersion for people who would never book a gallery. Retellability: literalising the metaphor, spirits into spirits, is a pun that does the memory work by itself; it is the Ice Watch one-sentence mechanism at cocktail scale, and it lodges in a delegate's head faster than any panel. Sensory translation away from the eye: scent carrying fragments of place history, and a collective distillation in which the audience makes the volatile archive together, which turns reception into co-authorship and gives the delegates something they did with their hands to talk about. What I would have done differently is the ask and the trace. A conference that will issue statements is the easiest place in the world to route noticing to action: a line about the organisms who bore the risk, tabled by the artists, adopted or refused on record. And I would have kept a bottle — a distillate, labelled, in the Science History Institute's collection — so the decay bridge has a carrier that outlasts the evening.
gist: Insert the work into the institution's own ritual, literalise the metaphor for retellability, and let delegates co-distil the archive; it needed a tabled ask and a bottle in the collection.

text: Reaching a hundred decision-makers is worth more than reaching ten thousand visitors, and it reproduces the elite access the 1975 meeting is criticised for: an invitation-only conference with a public lecture attached, where marginal spirits are served by artists who were themselves invited. The artists choose which ghosts drink — the place, the lab organisms, the women staff — and the organisms gain symbolic presence with no way to correct the flavour they have been given; that is authorship over the dead dressed as hospitality. The tension I feel most is institutional. Art and culture were built into the programme, which means the work is also the line item that lets a governance meeting feel reflective, and I have watched that happen at climate summits. The stronger the aesthetics of sacrifice — lab animals as a cocktail note — the easier to toast them and move to the next session. Add the mundane politics of drinks and scents: allergy, consent, readings of intoxication at a professional event. None of this argues against the piece, which I admire; it is the cost of platform dependence, where the host owns both the room and the story of what the evening meant.

text: For an academic project the reach is real: a free drop-in gallery at Summerhall during the Edinburgh Science Festival for two weeks, and seven lunchtime dining sessions with forty-seven people across ages, ethnicities and professions who were not recruited from a design department. The epistemic bridge is where I stop. The hybrids are fictional — the menu is entirely speculative apart from allergens, the real food is vegan sourdough, miso and kraut — so what becomes perceivable is not a microbe's condition but the diner's own moral shortcuts: cannibalism, consent, risk, whether somebody got paid. The paper is candid that this is the point. But the actual microbes present, the lactobacilli in the kraut and the yeast in the bread, are the least noticed beings in the room; the theatre is about people, and the microbe is a proxy's proxy. No action is asked, the magnets are not data by the authors' own statement, and the decay bridge is the CHI paper and whatever forty-seven people said at dinner that night. Everyday invisibility of the organisms we eat is named and then left where it was.

text: Ingestion is the most consequential embodied juxtaposition in this portfolio: you cannot un-eat, so moral weighing has a bodily aftermath — the authors' decisions that had to be stomached. Around it is an invitation outfit — lab coat at the door, antique scales, petri dishes for bread, a narrating host — that turns a festival lunch into a role, and a menu that is narrative fiction with a joke per line: moral allergens beside gluten, Metabolic Manacles Fougasse, Corporate Kraut. The magnets and scales are a designed non-utility function: the task is to quantify moral weight, and its point is that people discover they cannot — several called it an impossible calculus. I keep thinking of MIT's Moral Machine, which got millions to rank lives online and found they put cats and dogs below criminals; this puts forty-seven people at a table and makes them feel the same valuation gap in their mouths. That is the tactic I would borrow — enact the scale rather than survey it. I would also take the menu online as a Moral Machine for microbes, so the enactment gets the reach the theatre cannot, and keep the dinner as the deep end.
gist: Eating as the most consequential juxtaposition, a lab-coat-and-scales invitation outfit, a menu of fictional biographies with humour, and a deliberately impossible calculus enacted rather than surveyed.

text: Climate refugees' sweat glands, cancelled journalists' blood, a diabetic donor, deformed broiler chickens: human and animal suffering is the flavouring that gives microbial labour emotional weight, and participants went where the menu pointed, to Gaza and genocide. The authors say the discomfort is deliberate and not an equation; I accept the intent and still call it appropriation, because the affect was borrowed from people who were not at the table. The second tension is that the study steered its own closures: in the first two sessions the hosts confirmed consent had been obtained and watched moral weight drop, then withheld it for the remaining five to see what people assumed. That is a designer rewriting the fiction between performances to harvest hesitation, and the paper's plea — make space for moral hesitation — sits oddly beside a method that manufactures it. Third, disgust is not ethics: four diners in session one judged by gross rather than wrong, as the paper admits. I agree with the note that this must not be written as affect improving ethics. The lasting political value is smaller: ready-made ethics close inquiry in under a minute, a fact about publics we should all design against.
gist: Human suffering used as flavouring for microbial sympathy is appropriation even when declared; the hosts changed the consent disclosure mid-run to harvest hesitation; disgust is not ethics.

text: The tactic is friction by design. Replacing pointed probes with two conductive fingertips forces a wiggling, digging alignment under leaf litter; the LED on the back of the hand gives an approximate reading you must earn. text: The interesting political tension here is about labour. Liu's line runs into Biggs, Bardzell and Bardzell, who treat the tedium and abjection of noticing as productive; I think noticing is a cost that design should lower, so this glove and I disagree at the root, and I want that disagreement in the paper rather than smoothed over. On fidelity the work is exemplary: it says it measures conductivity in substrate, not fungal presence or feeling, and it reports lower accuracy than a rigid probe. The authority problem is quieter: the calibration, two fingers pressed lightly, is designer-set, so what counts as "wet enough" is Liu's hand. Digging fingers into leaf litter and soil disturbs the very substrate being cared about, and the paper names the gesture's sexual and medical connotations without asking who is comfortable performing it, on top of forest access and mobility. No overclaim anywhere; the tension is that honesty this complete still leaves one transformed wearer.
gist: An honest, non-overclaiming prototype that treats noticing labour as productive, where I treat it as a cost; calibration authority, substrate disturbance and bodily access remain.
